s-params-001.question: Which correctly describes the S-parameter S11 of a two-port network?
choices: The ratio of the wave coming out of port 2 to the wave sent into port 1
The input impedance seen from port 1 when port 2 is left open
The ratio of the reflected wave to the incident wave at port 1 when port 2 is terminated in the reference impedance
s-params-001.explanation: S-parameters describe a network by the ratios of the waves b leaving and a entering each port. S11 = b1/a1 is the reflection coefficient at port 1 when port 2 is terminated in the reference impedance (usually 50 Ω), making a2 = 0. The ratio of the wave entering port 1 and leaving port 2 is S21, which corresponds to the gain of an amplifier or the transmission of a filter. Parameters defined under open- or short-circuit conditions are Z-parameters and Y-parameters. At high frequencies ideal opens and shorts are hard to make, which is why S-parameters, measured with matched terminations, are used.

s-params-002.question: When expressing the magnitude of an S-parameter in dB, which is the correct reason for using 20 log₁₀|S21| rather than 10 log?
choices: S-parameters are power ratios, so the value is doubled to add the two passes of the round trip
S-parameters are ratios of wave amplitudes proportional to voltage, and the power ratio is their square
Using 20 log makes the value always positive, even for lossy networks
s-params-002.explanation: The a and b in S-parameters are the amplitudes of incident and reflected waves formed from the voltage and current at each port, normalized so that |a|² corresponds to power. So |S21| is an amplitude ratio and the power ratio is |S21|². Since dB is defined on power ratios, 10 log₁₀|S21|² = 20 log₁₀|S21|; for example, an amplifier with |S21| = 10 has 20 dB of gain (100 times in power). The idea of adding two passes of a round trip is wrong: S21 describes a single one-way transmission. In a lossy network |S21| < 1, so its 20 log value is negative.

s-params-003.question: When S21 of a filter is −0.5 dB in its passband, which is closest to the fraction of the input power that reaches the output port (each port terminated in the reference impedance)?
choices: About 89%
About 94%
About 11%
s-params-003.explanation: The power ratio is 10^(−0.5/10) = 10^(−0.05) ≈ 0.891, so about 89% reaches the output port. The remaining 11% or so is either reflected back toward the input or turned into heat inside the filter. About 94% is the amplitude ratio |S21| = 10^(−0.5/20) ≈ 0.944; to get power you must square it. About 11% is the fraction that does not arrive. Insertion loss is expressed as −20 log₁₀|S21|, so this example has 0.5 dB of insertion loss. It looks small, but placed at the front of a receiver it worsens the noise figure by about 0.5 dB directly.

s-params-004.question: For a passive network made only of resistors, capacitors, inductors and lines (with no magnetic materials such as ferrite and no active devices), which relation always holds?
choices: S21 = S12 (reciprocity)
s-params-004.explanation: A network made only of linear, isotropic materials such as resistors, L, C and lines satisfies the reciprocity theorem, so its S-matrix is symmetric and S21 = S12: the transmission is the same in either direction. S11 = S22 holds only when the network is physically symmetric. |S11|² + |S21|² = 1 is the condition for a lossless network; in a network containing resistance, some power becomes heat, so the sum is less than 1. Circulators and isolators using ferrite with a DC magnetic field, and transistor amplifiers, have S21 ≠ S12.

s-params-005.question: For a lossless, reciprocal two-port with port 2 terminated in a matched load, |S11| = 0.6. What is |S21|?
s-params-005.explanation: In a lossless network the incoming power is only divided between reflection and transmission, so |S11|² + |S21|² = 1. |S21| = √(1 − 0.6²) = √0.64 = 0.8, or about −1.9 dB. 0.4 is the mistake of subtracting the amplitudes directly (1 − 0.6); conservation of power must be applied to squared amplitudes. 0.64 is |S21|², the power transmission (64%). The reflected power is 0.36, or 36%, and with no loss the total is exactly 100%.

s-params-006.question: The S11 of an antenna was measured as −10 dB. What fraction of the incident power is reflected?
choices: About 32%
s-params-006.explanation: S11 = −10 dB means |S11| = 10^(−10/20) ≈ 0.316, and the reflected power is |S11|² = 0.1, or 10%. Reading the dB value as a power ratio gives 10^(−10/10) = 0.1 directly. About 32% confuses the amplitude ratio 0.316 with a power fraction, and 1% is the value for −20 dB. In this case the remaining 90% enters the antenna (a mismatch loss of about 0.46 dB), and the VSWR is (1 + 0.316)/(1 − 0.316) ≈ 1.9. Antenna bandwidth is often quoted as the range where S11 is −10 dB or lower, but the required value depends on the application.

s-params-007.question: +30 dBm is fed into the input port of a directional coupler with 20 dB coupling. What power comes out of the coupled port (assume an ideal coupler)?
choices: +1.5 dBm
+10 dBm
+50 dBm
s-params-007.explanation: The coupling C is the ratio of the coupled-port power to the input power; in dB you subtract, giving 30 − 20 = +10 dBm (10 mW). The input is 1 W, so this is 1/100 of it. +1.5 dBm is the mistake of dividing dBm by dB (30/20); dividing dB values by each other has no meaning. +50 dBm is the mistake of adding the attenuation. Since the coupled port takes 1% of the power, 99% comes out of the through port, a loss of only 10 log₁₀(1/0.99) ≈ 0.04 dB. Weakly coupled couplers like this are used to monitor transmitter output.

s-params-008.question: A directional coupler has a coupling of 20 dB and an isolation (attenuation from the input port to the isolated port) of 50 dB. What is its directivity?
choices: 70 dB
2.5 dB
30 dB
s-params-008.explanation: Directivity is the ratio, for the same forward wave entering the input port, of the power at the coupled port to the power leaking to the isolated port. In dB it is the isolation minus the coupling: D = I − C = 50 − 20 = 30 dB. 70 dB is the mistake of adding them, and 2.5 dB divides one dB value by the other. With low directivity, part of the forward wave mixes in when you want to extract only the reflected wave, which sets a lower limit on the reflection you can measure. With a 30 dB directivity coupler, for loads whose return loss is around 30 dB or more (smaller reflections), the reflected wave and the leakage are of similar size and become hard to tell apart.

s-params-009.question: For an equal-split, two-way Wilkinson divider in a 50 Ω system, which combination of characteristic impedance for the two λ/4 lines and resistor between the two outputs is correct?
choices: Lines of about 70.7 Ω and a 100 Ω resistor
Lines of 50 Ω and a 50 Ω resistor
Lines of about 35.4 Ω and a 25 Ω resistor
s-params-009.explanation: Each output is terminated in 50 Ω, and from the input the two branches appear in parallel. To match the input to 50 Ω, each branch must look like 100 Ω at the input, so the quarter-wave transformer formula gives Z = √(50 × 100) = 50√2 ≈ 70.7 Ω. The resistor between the outputs is 2Z0 = 100 Ω. With 50 Ω lines, each branch looks like 50 Ω, or 25 Ω in parallel, which is a mismatch. 35.4 Ω is 50/√2, dividing by √2 where you should multiply. Ideally each output is at −3.01 dB, and high isolation is obtained between the two outputs.

s-params-010.question: Which correctly describes the role of the resistor placed between the two output ports of a Wilkinson divider?
choices: It provides isolation between the output ports and absorbs waves returning from the output side
It always dissipates half of the input power as heat to stabilize the split ratio
It splits a DC bias between the two outputs
s-params-010.explanation: When both output ports are matched and carry the same signal, the two ends of the resistor are at the same potential, so no current flows and, ideally, there is no loss. If a reflection occurs at one output port or a signal enters from outside, that wave reaches the other output by two paths — through the resistor, and through the two λ/4 lines with a half-wavelength phase difference — and the two cancel. This gives isolation between the outputs, and the canceled power becomes heat in the resistor. A divider that always dissipates power is the resistive splitter made only of resistors. Supplying bias is not the purpose of the resistor.

s-params-011.question: Which statement about a three-port circulator is correct?
choices: It is a reciprocal device that divides power entering any port equally between the other two ports
It is a nonreciprocal device that passes power only in the direction port 1 → 2 → 3 → 1, and terminating one port in a matched load turns it into an isolator
It is an active device using transistors, so it does not work without a DC supply
s-params-011.explanation: A circulator uses the properties of a ferrite under a DC magnetic field to pass signals only in one rotational direction: 1 → 2, 2 → 3, 3 → 1. It is a nonreciprocal network with S21 ≠ S12, because the magnetic material breaks reciprocity. Terminating port 3 in a matched load gives an isolator that passes 1 → 2 while absorbing reflections returning from 2 in the termination at 3; this is used to protect a transmitter's power amplifier from reflections. Connecting a transmitter, an antenna and a receiver to the ports also lets it separate transmit from receive. It is magnetized by a permanent magnet, so it is a passive device needing no power supply. Equal division is the job of a divider.

s-params-012.question: When finding the overall characteristics of two-port networks connected in cascade, which is the correct advantage of using ABCD matrices (also called chain or transmission matrices)?
choices: The overall matrix is found simply by adding the ABCD matrices of each stage
Multiplying the S-parameter matrices of each stage directly gives the overall S-parameters
The overall matrix is found simply by multiplying the ABCD matrices of each stage in the order they are connected
s-params-012.explanation: An ABCD matrix expresses the voltage and current at port 1 in terms of the voltage and outgoing current at port 2. Because the output voltage and current of the first stage become the input of the second, a cascade is found from the product of the stage matrices. Matrix multiplication depends on order, so multiply in the order of signal flow. Adding matrices works for Z-matrices of series connections and Y-matrices of parallel connections. S-parameters are ratios of incident and reflected waves, so multiplying them directly does not give the cascade; convert them to T-matrices (transfer scattering matrices) or ABCD matrices first.

s-params-013.question: What is the ABCD matrix of a two-port consisting of a single series impedance Z? The matrix is written in the order [A B; C D].
s-params-013.explanation: With a series impedance, the current passes straight through, so I1 = I2, and the voltages differ by the drop across Z, so V1 = V2 + Z·I2. Comparing with V1 = A·V2 + B·I2 and I1 = C·V2 + D·I2 gives A = 1, B = Z, C = 0, D = 1. [1 0; 1/Z 1] is the matrix of a shunt Z; there the voltages are equal, V1 = V2, and the current splits as I1 = V2/Z + I2. [Z 0; 0 1] would mean that with Z = 0 (a plain wire) no voltage is transmitted, which is absurd. For a reciprocal network AD − BC = 1, and [1 Z; 0 1] satisfies this.

s-params-014.question: A 50 Ω resistive source and a 200 Ω resistive load are matched with an L-network using one series reactance and one shunt reactance. What is the Q of the circuit (the loaded Q)?
s-params-014.explanation: The Q of an L-network is fixed by the ratio of the resistances being transformed: Q = √(Rhigh/Rlow − 1) = √(200/50 − 1) = √3 ≈ 1.73. The series element has a reactance Xs = Q·Rlow ≈ 86.6 Ω, and the shunt element Xp = Rhigh/Q ≈ 115 Ω. 4 is the resistance ratio itself, and 2 is √(200/50), forgetting to subtract 1. In an L-network, Q is set by the resistance ratio and cannot be chosen freely; the larger the ratio, the higher the Q and the narrower the bandwidth. To widen the bandwidth, use several L-sections with a smaller ratio in each; to narrow it, use a π- or T-network for a higher Q.

s-params-015.question: On a Smith chart (impedance chart), how does the impedance point move as inductance is added in series with a load?
choices: It moves counterclockwise along a constant-resistance circle, toward the lower half (capacitive)
It moves clockwise along a constant-resistance circle, toward the upper half (inductive)
It moves along a constant-conductance circle, changing the resistance
s-params-015.explanation: Adding a series inductor leaves the resistance R unchanged and increases only the reactance, by +jωL. The set of points with constant resistance is a constant-resistance circle, so the point moves clockwise along that circle toward the upper half (the inductive +j side). Moving counterclockwise toward the lower half happens when a series capacitor (−j/ωC) is added. Moving along a constant-conductance circle happens when an element is added in shunt, changing only the susceptance of the admittance. In L-network matching, elements are chosen so that you follow a constant-resistance circle and a constant-conductance circle in turn and arrive at the center (z = 1).
